newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-Japan ex-minister wary on reform outlook.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Japan ex-minister wary on reform outlook.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has donned a reformist mantle, but a stroll down the corridors of power has left one former cabinet minister with doubts about Hashimoto's true intentions.

"The question is, does Hashimoto really intend to tackle (reform) through political leadership? Frankly, that is open to doubt," Shusei Tanaka, Economic Planning Agency (EPA) minister in Hashimoto's first cabinet, told Reuters in an interview.

An adviser to then-prime minister Morihiro Hosokawa, whose awkward coalition booted out the long-dominant Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) in 1993, Tanaka was one architect of Hosokawa's platform urging deregulation and structural reform.

After political feuding fractured the anti-LDP bloc and set the stage for the party's return to power in a tripartite coalition, Tanaka -- a member of the tiny Sakigake Party -- was tapped as EPA chief in Hashimoto's cabinet in January 1996.

Few would have seen Hashimoto or the LDP as key advocates of change, but with mounting domestic pressure to revise old-style practices now seen as obstacles to future economic success, the party began echoing critics' calls for reform.
Tanaka became Hashimoto's public point man on deregulation in a campaign which proclaimed that politicians had seized the initiative and would bring recalcitrant bureaucrats to heel.

But his 10 months in office, which ended when he lost his Lower House seat in the October 1996 polls, have left Tanaka doubtful about prospects for deregulation and other government reforms that Hashimoto has made his rallying cry.

Hashimoto, with an all-LDP cabinet, has pledged in his second term to push through change in six key areas. These areas include "administrative reform", a vague term encompassing such goals as cutting government agencies down to size and eliminating bureaucratic interference in economic matters.

How likely is Hashimoto to effect such changes? Perhaps not very, Tanaka says, given the long-standing tangle of ties that bind him and most politicians to the same bureaucrats whose ways they have promised to mend.

"Politicians are like cats who are indebted to mice," Tanaka said. "So when the mice misbehave right in front of them, the cats turn a blind eye. Politicians have lost the ability to act as a check on bureaucrats."

"Hashimoto has for a long time occupied positions of power and responsibility, so by force of circumstance he has continued such ties (with bureaucrats). Common sense tells us he can't cut them quickly," Tanaka said.

Official misdeeds, including an AIDS scandal at the Health Ministry and the latest admissions of cover-ups of nuclear mishaps by a state-run firm, have ignited public pressure for change, Tanaka said.
But predicting whether Japan will meet the challenges posed by the need for sweeping reforms is hard to say, he added.

"The time when Japan might 'sink' is approaching more rapidly, but at the same time, the opportunity for change is also approaching more rapidly. I'm neither optimistic nor pessimistic. It's impossible to say."
